strengths: Continuous-domain Pareto-set identification under noisy evaluations is a well-motivated problem with an identifiable audience in Bayesian optimization and active learning.

The algorithm combines region-wide uncertainty bounds, inherited confidence rectangles, pessimistic Pareto comparisons, and a refinement-versus-evaluation rule in a coherent framework. The conditional coverage arguments provide useful insight into preserving coverage through successive discards.

Considering dependent GP outputs and developing both information-gain and metric-dimension analyses are worthwhile contributions. The high-level explanations, illustrations, and organized appendix help readers understand the intended approach.

The experiments include ten sampled functions with five runs each, four relevant competitors including qNEHVI, and measurements of both prediction quality and runtime. The reported MSE results and substantial dependence on tree depth provide encouraging preliminary evidence.
weaknesses: Necessary: Theorem 1's guarantee needs a corrected derivation. In Corollary 1, the chosen u contains h log N and Lemma 7 uses 2u, but the stated V_h contains only h log N. Moreover, V_0 contains log(0), although the algorithm starts at depth zero. Lemma 14, equations (31) and (33), assumes that a previously refined parent satisfies the refinement threshold using the current beta; the threshold held at the earlier refinement time, and increasing beta need not preserve it. A proof using inherited rectangles may resolve the latter issue. Propositions 4 and 5 also need a valid argument over evaluation prefixes: Lemma 3 supplies a sufficient termination condition and does not justify their stated stopping-time inference. These unresolved steps affect the central correctness and sample-complexity claims.

Necessary: Proposition 1 and Appendix C do not establish the claimed linear information gain. The displayed lower bound contains a_Tj²/(a_Tj² + sigma²), which depends on T, so it does not imply Omega(T). Keeping the independent bump variances bounded away from zero would create infinitely many uniformly separated points in the GP-induced metric, conflicting with compactness and Assumption 1. Simply asserting that a suitable metric exists does not resolve this conflict. Remove or replace this proposition and revise the claims about separation between the two complexity bounds.

Necessary: The empirical metrics in Section 7.1 are inconsistent with Definitions 3–5. A severely suboptimal point can be epsilon-dominated by a true Pareto point, so the stated operational accuracy test does not establish membership in Z_epsilon. Membership instead excludes points q for which some Pareto value z satisfies q + 2epsilon <= z. The coverage description also switches between epsilon and 2epsilon as though they were equivalent. Provide the exact implemented predicates and reconcile the results with the definitions. Report accuracy and coverage separately; their average in Table 2 obscures the two required properties. A mean score near 99% also does not establish the theorem's probability of simultaneous success across the returned set.

Necessary: Clearly qualify the guarantees and practical conclusions for the capped-depth variants. Setting V_h = 0 for cells of positive width removes the protection against within-cell variation, so Theorem 1 does not apply to these variants as described. The depth-24 configuration takes 15:15:24 versus 00:00:40 for qNEHVI. The depth-9 configuration is faster, but its MSE is 40 versus 10 in the table's units. These are meaningful tradeoffs rather than general performance dominance. Restrict empirical conclusions to the tested one-dimensional, two-independent-objective GP setting unless additional evidence supports broader claims.

Necessary clarification: Algorithm 1 computes the pessimistic Pareto set on line 3 before constructing the current rectangles on lines 4–7, although Definition 8 requires those rectangles. Reconcile the pseudocode with the procedure used in the proofs and implementation, and define root-parent handling. For reproducibility, explain how finite predictions are extracted from the returned union of cells, how baseline predictions are constructed, and how confidence intervals account for the ten-function/five-run sampling structure.

Optional improvements: A fixed-grid variant using the same GP model and decision rules would help isolate the benefit of adaptive discretization. Experiments with correlated objectives and higher-dimensional inputs would clarify practical reach. Streamlining repeated novelty assertions and the duplicated runtime discussion would improve readability. These extensions are optional if the claims are appropriately narrowed; the recommendation is driven by the unresolved correctness and evaluation issues above.
